newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: AUTOMAKERS SOARS ON FOREIGN TIE-UP RUMOURS.
newsitem.headline: AUTOMAKERS SOARS ON FOREIGN TIE-UP RUMOURS.

text.p: Shares in South African car maker Automakers Ltd soared again on Friday amid a swirl of rumours that the firm is in talks with Japan's Nissan and Italy's Fiat on a possible tie-up.
On Thursday the share jumped 76 cents to 2.80 rand and the upward momentum followed through into Friday as by 1045 GMT the stock had put on another 45 cents to 3.25 rand.

The rapid rise forced the firm to put out a cautionary statement urging shareholders not to trade in the company's stock as certain developments currently being contemplated could have a material impact on its share price.
The statement made no mention of the other companies involved, but dealers and analysts said all the talk was about the two international motor giants.
"It is all rumours but something must be going on," said one analyst who declined to be identified.

Automakers' communications director Johan Kleynhans told Reuters he could not confirm the company was in talks with either or both of the two firms and declined to elaborate beyond the information given in the cautionary statement.
"There is nothing more to add at this stage," he said.
Kleynhans added that a further announcement is expected early next week, but that it would be in the form of an update, not a complete deal.

Automakers main subsidiary Nissan SA has licensed its name from the Japanese group and the firm also sells Fiat's Uno model. Dealers and analysts have speculated one or both of the firms are in talks with Automakers' main shareholder Sankorp over the sale of its 50.7 percent stake.
"All I know is that Sankorp is around the table talking about a whole list of options," one analyst said.

Some analysts said Nissan was tipped to strike a deal by itself, but other said a tie-up with both firms would make more sense as they occupied complementary market niches. Nissan is not represented in the lower end of the narket and Fiat has no presence in the upper end.
Nissan declined to comment on any move for Automakers. "We cannot make any comment because it is related to the stock market," a Nissan spokeswoman told Reuters in Tokyo.
The deal would mirror a move in October by Japan's Toyota Motor Corp when that firm bought a 27.8 pecent stake in Toyota SA for 446 million rand.
That deal first sparked talk of a similar move involving Nissan SA.

Analysts say this kind of deal is good for overseas groups as, with an eye to future growth, it gives them access to emerging markets. The local firm, however, also benefits with improved access to new technology and export opportunites.
Most major foreign firms withdrew operations from South Africa during the apartheid era, but a trend has emerged for groups to buy back their former subsidiaries or brandname holders.
Last year tyre giant Goodyear , industrial firm Owens Corning and drugs group American Home Products all returned to the country by buying back former units or products.
